notes.meaning: God shows Amos a vision of a locust swarm being prepared to destroy the fields. This happens after the king took his tax from the first harvest, right when the people's main food crop was beginning to sprout. If this second crop was wiped out, the everyday people would face terrible famine until the next year.

Amos watches the locusts strip away the green plants, and he begs God to forgive the nation. He calls the people by the name of Jacob, reminding God of His ancient covenant promise to a weak and humble forefather. Even though Israel felt rich and successful at the time, Amos knew they were too frail to survive God's punishment.

The Lord listens to the prophet's plea and promises that this destruction will not take place. God spares the land out of His great mercy before the disaster can fall. This shows the wonderful power of intercession, which means praying to God on behalf of other people.

differ.view: Believers in this tradition teach that God's eternal decree never changes, so the Bible uses words about God relenting to describe how His outward actions look to human beings.
Many Christians take these words more simply, believing that God truly responds to earnest prayer by altering what He decides to do in history.

notes.meaning: God gives Amos a second vision, this time calling down a fierce fire of judgment. The blaze is so severe that it dries up the deep underground waters and begins eating up Israel's land. It represents a harsher punishment than the locusts, picturing a killing drought or the burning destruction of war.

Amos cries out again for the Lord to stop the disaster before the whole nation is consumed. He repeats his plea that Jacob is small and unable to stand up against such intense wrath. A faithful messenger always feels deep sorrow for the people facing God's judgment.

The Lord answers Amos a second time and agrees to hold back the consuming fire. He declares that this disaster will not happen either. God shows tremendous patience by giving a stubborn people another chance to turn from their sins.

The Lord shows Amos a third vision, standing beside a straight wall with a plumb line in His hand. A plumb line is a string with a lead weight that builders use to check if a wall is straight and vertical. God had built Israel to be upright, but now He has come to test how crooked the nation has become.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the rare Hebrew word here may mean tin rather than a plumb line, presenting a vision of a flimsy tin wall instead of a measuring tool.

notes.meaning: God tells Amos that He is placing the plumb line right among His people to measure them against His true standard of justice. Because Israel is dangerously out of line and refuses to repent, God announces that He will no longer spare them. Amos does not pray to stop this judgment, realizing that the nation has run out of time.

The Lord declares that Israel's religious shrines and altars will be wiped out. The people boasted in their family ties to Isaac, but their worship had been ruined by idol worship. God also promises to attack the royal family of King Jeroboam with the sword, which led to the end of his dynasty.

Amaziah, the leading priest at the idol center in Bethel, sends a warning message to King Jeroboam of Israel. He accuses Amos of plotting treason against the king right out in the open. He claims the land cannot handle the harsh warnings Amos is preaching.

Amaziah tries to turn the king against Amos by exaggerating what the prophet actually said. He claims Amos predicted the king himself would die by the sword, even though Amos had only spoken against Jeroboam's family line. Worldly leaders often twist the truth when they want to silence a godly message.

Amaziah orders Amos to run away to his home territory in Judah. He mocks Amos as a visionary and tells him to go make his living and preach down south where people might pay him. The priest assumes Amos is only prophesying for money because that is how Amaziah himself lives.

The priest commands Amos never to preach at Bethel again because it belongs to the king and his royal court. Amaziah views the shrine as a state business and political symbol rather than a place belonging to God. He thinks human royal authority has the right to control where God's truth is spoken.

Amos answers that he was never a professional prophet, nor was he raised in a school of prophets. He was simply a sheep farmer and a field worker who took care of common sycamore-fig trees. He had an honest trade and was not preaching to gain money or social status.

Amos explains that the Lord Himself called him directly from tending the sheep and sent him to preach to Israel. His authority did not come from human credentials or a government license, but from God's direct command. When God calls someone to speak, no earthly ruler has the power to silence them.

Amos turns directly to Amaziah and tells him to hear God's verdict. The priest had ordered Amos to stop pouring out God's warnings against the northern tribes. By trying to plug up the flow of God's message, Amaziah had picked a fight with God Himself.

Amos announces a terrible doom on Amaziah's personal family and property when the foreign invaders attack. The priest's wife will be disgraced in the city, his children will be killed in war, his land will be handed to foreigners, and he will die in an unclean pagan country. Amos finishes by repeating the very warning Amaziah tried to silence: the people of Israel will certainly be carried off into exile.
